lines.text: Ever watched the price break a level, stop you out, then fly the other way? That's a liquidity sweep.
In trading, liquidity just means orders waiting to be filled. And the biggest piles sit where the crowd thinks alike.
Look at these two equal lows. Everyone sees support. So everyone puts their stop loss right underneath.
That pile has a name: sell-side liquidity. Every stop is a sell order, waiting to fire.
Now a big fund wants to buy a million shares. But on the shelves, only forty thousand are for sale.
If they just buy, the price runs away from them. They need a crowd of sellers, all at once.
So the price gets pushed down through the lows. Stops fire, sell orders flood in, and the fund soaks up every share.
Order filled. No sellers left. The price snaps back above the lows.
On the chart you only see one candle. A long wick under the lows, and a close back inside.
A real breakdown keeps going and closes below. A sweep pokes through, and closes back inside. That close is the tell.
Flip it. Above equal highs sits buy-side liquidity: the stops of short sellers. Sweep those, and the price drops.
Not financial advice. But next time, don't park your stop exactly under the obvious low.
Send this to a friend on Orbi Transfer. Now you know!
